title: Stop for Big Moments!
principle: Add hit stop so attacks feel heavy
why: A brief stop in the action when a hit lands completely changes how heavy the hit feels.
how: Freeze the action for a brief moment when an attack connects, and compare with and without it.
anti_pattern: Skimping on stop effects as minor polish.
quote: Whether or not it's there will completely change how heavy a hit feels, so it's a pretty important effect.

title: Stop for Big Moments!
principle: Stop and flash the screen when a boss is defeated
why: His 'boss stop' is vital for letting the player really feel the impact of beating a boss.
how: On boss defeat, freeze the screen and flash it for a moment before the defeat sequence plays.
example: Kirby's Adventure (NES) boss defeats; Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's Finish Zoom extends the idea.
quote: When you defeat a boss, the screen stops and flashes for a moment. This is vital for letting the player really feel that impact.

title: Stop for Big Moments!
principle: Freeze the action when the player gets hit or dies
why: In many scrolling shoot 'em ups players die without realizing; 'Wait, I got hit?' only tells them something is wrong, which is a missed opportunity. A pause shows the point of impact and gives an 'oh no!' feeling.
how: Pause the game for an instant when the player takes damage or loses a life so the point of impact is visible.
anti_pattern: Letting players die without seeing what happened.
example: Fantasy Zone (1986) stops the screen for a second on hit; Defender (1980) builds a stop into its hit effect.
quote: The takeaway shouldn't be, "Wait, I got hit?" That just tells you that something's wrong.

title: Stop for Big Moments!
principle: Layer stop, shake and slow motion at big moments
why: Stopping is one of many tools, and these effects let players feel moments of success or defeat; they are relatively easy to implement.
how: For the biggest moments, combine a screen stop with screen shake and slow motion.
example: Shooting-game footage shown with no effects, then with stop, shake and slow motion added.
quote: In your game's big moments, stop! Let your players feel those moments of success—or defeat.

title: Frame Rates
principle: Treat frames as your unit of time when tuning motion
why: In games, frames are often the unit of time, and since distance = time × speed, time has a huge effect on how far and fast things move.
how: Specify movement and action timings in frames at your target frame rate and tune speeds with that in mind.
quote: In games, these frames are often used as a unit of time. Distance = Time × Speed.

title: Frame Rates
principle: Target 60 fps when possible; accept 30 fps when visuals need it
why: 60 and 30 fps differ in look and in how smoothly they control; drawing twice as many frames sacrifices half your visual performance, and 30 fps is still more than adequate.
how: Choose the target frame rate early by weighing control smoothness against the rendering budget.
example: Side-by-side 60 fps vs. 30 fps footage.
quote: 60 fps is an ideal frame rate when possible, but 30 fps is also a common standard.

title: Down with Lag!
principle: Check input lag on every demo and test setup yourself
why: At E3 2018 the setup crew must have tested Smash Ultimate, yet nobody noticed lag bad enough to ruin the controls; many people don't recognize lag.
how: Press jump in a game that responds instantly (an NES game, not a 3D one) on the actual setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press.
anti_pattern: Assuming a setup is fine because someone else already played on it.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate at E3 2018 Treehouse: Live.
quote: Even though the setup crew must have tested the game out before the event, nobody noticed the lag.

title: Giving "Weight" to Buttons
principle: Tune on-screen response to set how heavy buttons feel
why: The same button press can feel light or heavy depending on movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag and frame rate; players somehow feel feedback with their hands.
how: Decide each character's intended weight and tune speed, inertia and jump physics to it, counting lag and frame rate as part of feel.
anti_pattern: Assuming feel comes only from physical hardware.
example: NES control pad games that feel radically different.
quote: Even with the same button presses, the response you see on-screen can make them feel so very different.

title: Giving "Weight" to Buttons
principle: Differentiate characters by speed, vulnerability and animation flair
why: Differences in movement speed, vulnerability and animation flair create the push and pull of versus matches and make characters feel wildly different in your hands.
how: Give each playable character a distinct mix of speed, vulnerability and animation style.
example: Super Smash Bros. fighters.
quote: Not only does this create the "push and pull" that makes for a fun versus match, it also makes for characters that feel wildly different in your hands.

title: Kirby Super Star
principle: In co-op scrollers, let the camera follow one lead player
why: In side-scrollers players pull each other along as they scroll, which breaks down with jumping and with copy abilities moving at very different speeds; focusing the screen on one lead solved it.
how: Make one player the camera's lead and warp any supporting player who drifts too far off-screen back to them.
anti_pattern: Letting all players scroll the screen with equal weight.
example: Kirby Super Star Helper system and Space Jump.
quote: Instead of letting both characters scroll the screen with equal weight, I placed the focus on only the lead character.

title: Super Smash Bros.
principle: Keep controls to a stick direction plus a button.
why: By 1996 fighting-game command inputs had become extremely complicated; simple inputs are something players can pick up intuitively.
how: Map moves to direction plus button, and use input timing, such as a quick stick flick, to trigger stronger attacks or jumps.
anti_pattern: Complex command inputs.
example: The smash input, a flick of the N64 analog stick.
quote: So I opted for simple controls with a stick direction and a button, something players could intuitively pick up.

title: Breaking Down Attack Animations
principle: Use hitstop to freeze the hit into a readable key pose.
why: Everything hinges on the moment an attack can hit; stopping the animation on contact makes that pose firm and readable.
how: Pause the animation when a hit lands so the attack pose holds on screen.
quote: You could say everything hinges on this moment.

title: Jump Physics
principle: Shape the jump's rise, fall and air control to your game's goals.
why: Mario's gentle rise and fast fall suits variable height, Samus's floaty jump helps with aiming, and Ghosts 'n Goblins' fixed arc makes every jump a plan.
how: Tune separate rise and fall acceleration and air control for what your game needs rather than using default physics.
anti_pattern: One generic jump for every game.
example: Super Mario Bros., Metroid and Ghosts 'n Goblins.
quote: Remember, though: your jump might change depending on the goal of your game.

title: Jump Physics
principle: Make descents faster than ascents to add impact.
why: Even with the same trajectory, adjusting a move's speed drastically changes how it feels.
how: For slams, throws or heavy landings, increase downward acceleration on the way down.
example: Zangief's Spinning Pile Driver from Street Fighter II Turbo onward.
quote: Even with the same trajectory, adjusting a move's speed can drastically change how it feels.

title: Jump Physics
principle: Keep a short, uniform windup before jumps when up-attacks share the input.
why: Without the windup, players would jump before they could input an Up Smash.
how: Add a short pre-jump windup and use the same length for every character.
anti_pattern: Removing the windup entirely.
example: Super Smash Bros.' unified jump windup.
quote: If we removed it entirely, players would end up jumping before they could input an Up Smash— so we have to keep it in some form.

title: Jump Physics
principle: Use a strong burst, then brief heavy gravity, for forgiving escape jumps.
why: Players can still get out of a jam even if they react a little late; the extra parameters and bug risk are worth it.
how: Apply very strong initial upward velocity, greatly increase downward acceleration for a few frames until the jump halts, then restore normal gravity.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate and Kirby Super Star.
quote: This way, players can still get out of a jam even if they react a little late.

title: A Small Window Into the World
principle: Budget how much of the screen your gameplay actually uses.
why: The screen covers only about 30 degrees of vision, so a wide view is squeezed into a narrow window and screen space is scarce.
how: Choose camera views that leave more room for play, and avoid views like cockpit cameras that shrink the usable area.
anti_pattern: Picking the most realistic camera at the cost of playable screen space.
example: Cockpit views in racing games.
quote: Back to the topic at hand, it's important to think about just how much screen space you're using for your gameplay.

title: A Small Window Into the World
principle: Use VR where viewpoint and direction of travel are separate.
why: VR's lower resolution blurs distant objects and you must turn your whole head, but it's a perfect fit when you look somewhere other than where you're moving.
how: Weigh the resolution and head-turning costs, and favor VR for games like racing where gaze and heading differ.
example: VR racing.
quote: Motion sickness is always a possibility, but for games that separate your viewpoint and direction of travel, VR is truly the perfect fit.

title: Eight Hit Stop Techniques
principle: Shake the victim more than the attacker, but never the hitbox
why: A pure stop works, but Sakurai always adds shake to sell the hit. If the hitbox shakes with the model, attacks that should connect end up missing.
how: During hit stop, offset only the rendered model: bigger amplitude on the victim, smaller on the attacker, horizontal-only on the ground (vertical shake makes legs clip the floor) and all directions in the air, decaying from big to small over the calculated duration.
anti_pattern: Moving the collision hitbox with the shake, or shaking grounded 3D characters vertically.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate hit stop
quote: As a general rule, hit stop in Smash Bros. is never just a stop— there's always a bit of "shake," too.

title: Eight Hit Stop Techniques
principle: Scale hit stop by attack strength and a per-move multiplier
why: Stronger attacks should feel stronger, and a multiplier on top lets a sweet spot feel heavier than its damage and lets guest characters match their original games.
how: Compute hit stop from damage, then multiply by a per-move or per-character factor; for example, give a sword tip a higher multiplier than its base. Lengthen it for lightning and reduce it in multiplayer.
example: Marth's Smash Attack (weak base, strong tip); Ryu's hit stops bigger and Kazuya's smaller at equal damage
quote: This isn't just a difference in attack values, but also the multiplier taking effect— making each hit feel even stronger than the damage dealt.

title: Eight Hit Stop Techniques
principle: Scale shake amplitude with camera distance
why: So the impact looks and feels the same whether the viewer is near or far.
how: When the camera is pulled back, make characters shake comparatively more than usual.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate camera-distance shake
quote: When the camera is pulled back, characters will shake comparatively more than usual.

title: The Potential of One Button
principle: Match controls to gameplay; don't add inputs just because you can
why: A single button can already do a great deal, each addition changes how the game feels, and the simplest approach often plays best.
how: Prototype the core action on one button using a tap, timing, reaction or hold/release pattern, and add another input only if it makes the game feel better.
anti_pattern: Adding control features just because you can.
example: Kirby's Adventure and Kirby Super Star one-button minigames
quote: Don't add more features just because you can— instead, consider how each addition will feel to the player.

title: Don't Anchor Your Center Point
principle: Don't track the camera center point fully on the Y axis
why: With the center point anchored to the character, it's really hard to tell how high they jump; letting them rise on screen lets players feel jump height.
how: Zero out or reduce Y-axis tracking during jumps so the character visibly moves up on screen.
anti_pattern: Anchoring the center point to the character's position by default.
example: Super Mario 64 jumping vs. a fighter-tracking camera in Smash Bros. Ultimate
quote: So, the center point shouldn't track on the Y axis— or should at least track less— to let players feel the height of their jumps.

title: Don't Anchor Your Center Point
principle: Let the character move off center to sell dodges and drifts
why: Moving away from the center makes dodged bullets and missiles visible, which is much more impactful, and in a drift it makes players really feel the input.
how: Offset the character from the center point in the direction of quick moves, dodges and drifts.
example: Armored Core movement; Kirby Air Ride drifting
quote: This makes it easier to see the bullets and missiles you've dodged, so it's much more impactful.

title: Don't Anchor Your Center Point
principle: Frame the camera to fit the gameplay, not just follow the character
why: Good framing improves presentation; side-scrollers want a wider view ahead, while realistic third-person racers may genuinely suit an anchored center point.
how: Choose framing per game: look-ahead for side-scrollers, anchored only where precision racing calls for it.
anti_pattern: Assuming the camera should always follow the character.
example: Side-scrollers; third-person racing games
quote: Don't assume the camera should always be following your character, but instead make sure it fits your gameplay and presentation.

title: Say No to Slow!
principle: Never let an unavoidable wait feel like a development mistake
why: Some load times can't be optimized away, but a wait that feels like someone dropped the ball is what irritates players.
how: Optimize loads as far as possible and make any remaining waits look deliberate rather than like an oversight.
anti_pattern: Waits that look like bugs or forgotten slowdowns.
quote: If that wait time feels like a mistake— like you're sitting around because someone dropped the ball in development— that's just irritating.

title: Learn to Count Frames!
principle: Learn to feel frames by counting "1-and-2-and" at 60 fps
why: Frames are the basis for all movement in games; with no stopwatch for frames, you need a trained sense to ballpark them.
how: Clap seconds saying "1-and-2-and-3-and": each beat is about 30 frames and half a beat about 15; check against an engine frame counter.
quote: Frames are the basis for all movement in games. That's why it's so important to learn how long they are.

title: Learn to Count Frames!
principle: Estimate frame counts relative to memorized reference moves
why: Approximating from known anchors is how to judge durations like 20 frames, which sits a little past halfway between 0 and 30.
how: Memorize reference timings from familiar games and estimate new values by their distance from the 0/15/30-frame anchors.
example: 15 frames is about a Smash Attack's input-to-release in Smash Bros. and a standard kick's startup in Tekken.
quote: We approximate based on how far we are from these reference points.

title: Follow-Throughs Make the Impact
principle: Give strong attacks proportionally long recovery
why: Lead-ins should be fast for responsiveness, but without vulnerability matching an attack's strength there is no push and pull and the game feels unrefined.
how: Have hits register about 1/4 to 1/3 into the move (1/5 for fast ones), keep moves under one second, and lengthen recovery as power rises.
anti_pattern: Powerful attacks with little vulnerability afterward.
example: Even Smash Bros. Smash Attacks with large vulnerability windows almost never exceed one second.
quote: But assuming you want push and pull, strong attacks should leave a character proportionally vulnerable afterward, or the game will feel really unrefined.

title: Follow-Throughs Make the Impact
principle: Place cancel frames where players expect to regain control
why: Cancel frames let the player act early during the return to standby, and their timing must match when people expect control back.
how: Mark a cancel window in the latter part of each recovery and playtest whether it lines up with players' instinctive timing.
example: Smash Bros. attack breakdowns mark where cancel frames end recovery.
quote: The timing of these cancel frames should fit with when people might expect they'll have control back.

title: Units of Speed
principle: Judge speed relative to the character's size
why: A speed that sounds slow in km/h is fast for a tiny character.
how: When tuning, compare speed to the character's own body size, not just the raw number.
example: Kirby Air Ride used km/h, and low-looking speeds were fast because Kirby is only a 20 cm square.
quote: These speeds might seem to be rather low, but that's because Kirby is only as big as a 20cm square.

title: Behavior at Ledges
principle: Decide ledge-falling per action instead of one global rule
why: Characters that always fall hurt many old games; Sakurai says letting some actions fall and others not is the way to do it.
how: Make forward dodges stop at edges while forward-rushing attacks carry over.
anti_pattern: Making characters fall off ledges regardless of conditions.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Fox Illusion stops at the ledge; Falcon Kick goes straight over.
quote: Falling off ledges isn't as straightforward as it seems.

title: Behavior at Ledges
principle: Never let small forward nudges drop players off ledges
why: If an action that nudges the character forward drops them off the ledge, it feels like their input was canceled.
how: Keep stepping attacks and similar small forward motions on the platform.
anti_pattern: Letting the slight forward motion of an attack carry the player over the edge.
quote: If you let a player fall off a ledge the moment they're nudged forward by an action, it may make them feel like their input was canceled—which isn't great.

title: Behavior at Ledges
principle: Gate ledge falls by momentum and move phase
why: Without accounting for momentum, it's too easy to go flying off the stage.
how: Make rushes stop at the ledge near the end of the move (Falcon Kick, Drill Rush) and set a speed threshold for rolling moves like Egg Roll.
anti_pattern: Ignoring momentum near edges.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Falcon Kick, Drill Rush, Yoshi's Egg Roll speed parameters.

title: Behavior at Ledges
principle: Help walking players at edges with push-to-fall or steering
why: Falling off ledges isn't straightforward; requiring a push against the ledge, or adjusting movement direction when the ledge is nearly parallel to it, are effective techniques.
how: Require continued input toward the edge before falling, or bend movement along near-parallel ledges; some games even auto-jump at ledges.

title: Screen Shake
principle: Use distinct shake patterns per impact size, not scaled copies
why: Smash's large, medium and small shakes aren't scaled versions of one shake but different patterns: small is vertical only, medium adds horizontal, large shakes more.
how: Author 3–4 shake presets with different axis behavior and map them to impact strength.
example: Super Smash Bros. large/medium/small/extra-small shakes.
quote: Large, medium, and small aren't just scaled versions of the same shake, but actually use different patterns entirely.

title: Screen Shake
principle: Scale shake to camera distance and field of view
why: Adjusting shake by camera distance keeps it from feeling off, and a tight field of view makes the usual shake feel really big.
how: Multiply shake amplitude by a camera-distance/FOV factor and retune scenes with unusual FOV.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Flat Zone's tighter field of view needed reduced shake.
quote: We change the size of the screen shake based on the distance of the camera.

title: Screen Shake
principle: Shake the camera's look-at point too, not just the camera
why: With 3D camera shake, distant objects barely move; if a far-off center point moves too subtly, it won't look like much is happening.
how: Sync the look-at point's shake with the camera, or shake it even more than the camera itself.
anti_pattern: Moving a distant center point so subtly that the shake doesn't read.

title: Screen Shake
principle: Start shakes strong and decay them with some randomness
why: A shake that starts strong, gradually subsides and isn't a clean whirlpool pattern feels nicer; too much shake makes the screen hard to see.
how: Use a decaying envelope with a slightly randomized path, and cap amplitude so the screen stays readable.
anti_pattern: Shaking so much that the screen becomes difficult to see.
example: Super Smash Bros. shake implementation.
quote: Even a tiny amount of shake can give attacks a drastically different impact.

title: Don't Be Unresponsive
principle: Give every button press some reaction
why: Information from the player's hands is vital, and an action with no reaction feels lacking; games are all about actions and reactions.
how: Audit each game state for dead buttons and give them a redundant function or at least visible feedback.
anti_pattern: Buttons that do nothing when pressed.
quote: Players press buttons because they want something from the game.

title: Don't Be Unresponsive
principle: Make press feedback unambiguous
why: Ambiguous responses that don't clearly show whether a button was pressed undermine the action-reaction loop.
how: Give each accepted press a distinct sound, highlight or animation.
anti_pattern: Feedback so subtle players can't tell if their press registered.
quote: It's also good to avoid ambiguous responses that don't clearly show whether a button was pressed.

title: Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Tune separate movement parameters for each very different mode
why: Dropping fighters into the Subspace Emissary with their Versus Mode specs didn't work.
how: Give characters a separate jump/movement parameter set per mode, and budget time to tune both sets.
anti_pattern: Reusing one mode's specs unchanged in a very different mode.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl: Subspace Emissary parameters.
quote: It didn't work just dropping fighters in with their specs from Versus Mode, so we made all sorts of adjustments.

title: Make Retries Quick
principle: Make losing feel impactful, but keep it to about a second
why: Players should really feel the loss, but dragging out the effect wastes the window when their interest is cooling.
how: Play a flashy, impactful failure effect lasting about one second (depending on genre), then return control as soon as possible.
anti_pattern: Dragging out the failure presentation.
quote: When the player loses, they should really feel it. Make the effect flashy and impactful, but get it over with quickly.

title: Family BASIC
principle: Learn game feel by tweaking movement code like inertia yourself
why: Toying with sprite inertia in Family BASIC let Sakurai see how different changes affect a game's feel, knowledge he drew on for Kirby's Dream Land.
how: Build a tiny controllable-character prototype and vary inertia and acceleration one value at a time, noting how each change feels.
anti_pattern: Relying on a convenient high-level movement command when you need responsive control; MOVE was limited to eight directions and lagged on input.
example: Family BASIC's SPRITE command: a controller-driven sprite with a little inertia.

title: Games During My Childhood
principle: Make the first moments of control direct, bright and flashy
why: Twisting a dial to move objects directly on a bright, flashy screen is what impressed young Sakurai about his first video games.
how: Make sure the player's first input immediately moves something clearly visible on an eye-catching screen.
example: Pong-style potentiometer games.

title: Motion Sickness in 3D Games
principle: Offer toggles for camera shake and other inertial embellishments
why: Sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear doesn't feel; turning off footstep shake can be very effective, but removing presentation for everyone makes the game less entertaining.
how: Add options to disable footstep vertical shake and other inertia-heavy camera effects rather than stripping presentation for everyone.
anti_pattern: Shipping strong camera inertia with no way to turn it off.
example: The common FPS option to toggle vertical shake from footsteps.
quote: Look at your game's presentation, and you'll find there's no harm in including options to counteract motion sickness.

title: Motion Sickness in 3D Games
principle: Lock on-screen vehicle frames in place, without inertial movement
why: A vehicle frame that sways adds visual motion with no matching physical motion; fixing it on screen reduces sickness.
how: Offer a mode where cockpit or vehicle frames are simply drawn on screen and don't move.

title: Hit Marks
principle: Keep hit-mark animations running through hitstop
why: Characters freeze during hitstop but effects can keep animating, so that window can carry extra detail.
how: Exclude hit-mark particles from the hitstop freeze and design them to unfold during it.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate; its hitstop direction-input effect shows the adjusted flight path.
quote: In most cases, hit marks can continue their animations even during the hit stop, so you should use that time to pack in even more detailed presentation.

title: Guidelines
principle: Keep a series' core rules and controls consistent across releases
why: Old Tetris games had no unified control scheme or rotation rules, so every version felt different, and changing the rules with every game makes it harder to play.
how: Standardize the fundamentals (piece colors and shapes, rotation points, preview count, ghost-piece display, lock behavior) and keep them identical across versions.
anti_pattern: Reinventing basic controls and rules in every new installment.
example: The Tetris Company's 2002 guidelines, which addressed infinite rotation delaying lockdown.
quote: But to be frank, changing the rules with every new game makes it harder to play.

title: Knockback in Super Smash Bros.
principle: Use fixed knockback on early hits of multi-hit moves
why: If the later hits failed to land because the opponent's damage was too low or too high, the move would break. Fixed knockback makes the reaction identical at any damage.
how: Give every hit but the last a fixed, damage-independent knockback, and give the finisher standard knockback.
anti_pattern: Damage-scaled knockback on the connecting hits of a multi-hit move.
example: Mario's Super Jump Punch.
quote: It would be quite the problem if later hits didn't land because the opponent's damage was too low or too high.

title: Knockback in Super Smash Bros.
principle: Guarantee a minimum knockback, kept in check by scaling
why: A launcher should cause at least some reaction on a barely damaged opponent, but simply adding a minimum would make knockback too big.
how: Add a per-attack minimum knockback value and pair it with knockback scaling, plus a multiplier for fine-tuning.
anti_pattern: Adding a flat minimum with no scaling, which inflates every launch.
example: Smash Bros. upward launch attacks against low-damage opponents.

title: Knockback in Super Smash Bros.
principle: Let knockback direction follow the attacker's travel to sustain aerial combos
why: Smash allows knockback in any direction, and a modifier that reacts to the attacker's movement helps more hits of an aerial combo land.
how: Give each attack a free launch angle plus an optional flag that biases the launch toward the attacker's direction of travel.
anti_pattern: Locking knockback to a few fixed directions when combos need to follow the target.
example: Smash Bros. aerial combos.

title: Make Important Elements Bigger
principle: Weight buttons unequally only when the game's actions are unequal
why: The GameCube's big A and small X/Y let you feel which button to press, but in games where all buttons have equal value that layout is harder to use and costs versatility.
how: Make the dominant action's input the most prominent, and keep inputs equal when the game uses them equally (e.g., face-button menu navigation).
anti_pattern: Unequal button emphasis in a game where every button matters equally.
example: The GameCube controller.

title: Flick Input
principle: Trigger dashes with a fast flick of the stick to its edge
why: Older dashes took two steps (double-tap) or two buttons (B-button dash). Reading how fast the stick reaches its edge gives one simple, physical action.
how: Scale walk speed by tilt, and start a dash when the stick travels from neutral to its edge within a short time.
anti_pattern: Requiring a double-tap or a held button for a basic movement action.
example: Super Smash Bros. (N64), where flick input was localized as "Tap."
quote: Adjusting walking speed based on how much you tilt the analog stick lets you not only feel the controls, but also understand them more easily.

title: Flick Input
principle: Make flick sensitivity adjustable to reduce accidental dashes
why: Flick input's downside is dashing by accident, and players differ in how hard they push the stick.
how: Expose the flick threshold as a player setting.
anti_pattern: A fixed threshold that causes unwanted dashes.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's flick sensitivity option.

title: Flick Input
principle: Explore a new peripheral's unique abilities, but don't shoehorn them in
why: New hardware can enable distinctive controls, as the analog stick did for Smash, but forcing every possible function in doesn't help the game.
how: List what the new input can do that older inputs can't and adopt only the uses that fit your design, e.g., one flick gesture for dash and dodge.
anti_pattern: Using every feature of a peripheral just because it's there.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's flick dash and dodge. Brawl deliberately not using every Nunchuk or pointer function.
quote: When designing games for hardware that features new peripherals, you should think for a moment about what's possible with those peripherals.

title: Special Crossover! #2
principle: Protect frame rate and display latency; they carry the game's feel
why: The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept every element in place but lost its smoothness and creepiness to a low frame rate, and modern TVs' image processing added enough lag to throw off Sakurai's shots.
how: Budget frame rate first when porting or downscaling, and playtest and record on a low-latency display with image processing off.
anti_pattern: Accepting a faithful but choppy port, or testing on a laggy TV.
example: Ghosts 'n Goblins arcade vs. NES; switching to the low-lag 'Mr. Sakurai Presents' monitor mid-session
quote: Today's monitors and TVs do a great deal of image processing.

title: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
principle: Retune every gameplay parameter whenever you change the game's tempo
why: Ultimate raised the tempo over Smash for (but kept it below Melee), and even jumps and knockback were sped up, which meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused.
how: When changing game speed, plan time to rebuild all movement and combat values instead of porting old ones.
anti_pattern: Carrying old tuning values into a faster game.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — tempo between Melee and Smash for
quote: It may sound simple, but increasing the game's tempo meant we couldn't reuse any of the parameters from Smash Bros. for.

title: It’s Easier If They Already Know
principle: Adopt your genre's de facto standard controls
why: Players who already know the conventions need no explanation, which warms up the handshake between human and computer.
how: Map core actions to the buttons the genre has standardized (as FPS games do with fire and grenade) unless you have a deliberate reason not to.
anti_pattern: Inventing a new layout only to avoid copying other games.
example: Western FPS games share nearly the same control scheme.
quote: By doing so, you're making the handshake between human and computer just a little bit warmer.

title: It’s Easier If They Already Know
principle: Always ship button remapping
why: Designers used to think their controls were the best and nobody would change them, but players want the freedom to play how they like.
how: Add a remapping option to the settings even though it makes things more complicated.
anti_pattern: Assuming your default layout is perfect for everyone.

title: What is “Play”?
principle: Imitate reality so objects and actions carry rich information
why: Mimicry increases the density and richness of a game's information because players read things the way they exist in reality.
how: Make floors look hard, windups look powerful and hits sound painful.

title: What is “Play”?
principle: Build visceral payoffs and fear into play
why: Ilinx, or vertigo, is what makes a game feel viscerally good.
how: Create strong knockback moments after a tough struggle and real danger around falling.
example: Knocking an enemy back after a tough struggle; the fear of falling.

title: Always Keep Attack Collision in Mind
principle: Make attack collision wider than the visible weapon in fast games
why: With fast, coordinate-based movement, hitboxes mapped tightly to a sword or fist make attacks miss and players get more and more stressed.
how: Extend hitboxes beyond the weapon and make sure every attack's range crosses the median line where opponents stand.
anti_pattern: Hitboxes that exactly match the blade or fist.
example: Smash Bros. attack collision covers a wider range than the fighter's sword or fist.

title: Speedy Screen Transitions
principle: Make screen transitions fast, but don't remove them entirely
why: Making players wait is a sin: slow fades and long black screens leave players without control and rob them of their time. It's almost impossible to be too fast, though cutting transitions entirely feels jarring.
how: Time every fade and black screen and trim each to a hasty speed that still reads as a transition.
anti_pattern: Slow, dreary fadeouts followed by lengthy black screens.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate uses random wipes to transition to the victory screen.
quote: A hasty speed is just right!

title: Speedy Screen Transitions
principle: Disguise loading behind transitions that fit the game and add mood
why: Many games use transitions to cover loading even without a loading icon, and done well they add to the experience, as Resident Evil's doors masked loading while creating fear.
how: Turn the loading cover into an in-world event (a door, a key) or a wipe that matches your theme, kept at an acceptable speed.
example: Original Resident Evil doors, which took longer to open when zombies were on the other side; Super Mario World's key transition adding mystery.
quote: There's always a way to make these things fit with your game.

title: Speedy Screen Transitions
principle: Scroll between fixed-camera screens so players see how the map connects
why: The first Zelda's edge-of-screen scrolling made a fixed camera easier to play with and showed how screens fit together, though today it could be smoother and faster.
how: Use a quick, smooth scroll for screen-to-screen movement instead of a cut or fade, and keep it from wasting time.
example: The Legend of Zelda (first game) edge scrolling.
quote: It's fundamental to both do what's right for your game, and make sure you're not wasting the player's time.

title: What Happens When You Shift the Center of Gravity?
principle: Add a looping wobble to straight-flying projectiles
why: A cannonball flying in a straight line isn't interesting to look at; sliding the sprite around in a loop makes the shot feel completely different.
how: Layer a six-frame positional loop (up, right-up, right-down, down, left-down, left-up) onto the projectile's path.
example: Kirby's Shotzo and its "wobbly cannonballs," which also suited the Game Boy screen's afterimages.
quote: If we simply sent the cannonballs flying forward in a straight line, it wouldn't be too interesting to look at.
